object_description: hexagonal four-storey solitaire with a recessed parapet and three vertical cores
design_condition: the hexagonal volume is set to define the northern schoolyard precisely while mediating between the large-scale residential buildings and the small-scale pavilion school, keeping the complex permeable

positive: The hexagonal volumetry responds to the specific situation
The four-storey structure with recessed parapet creates a coherent urban design with the heritage buildings
It mediates between the large-scale residential buildings and the small-scale pavilion school
The northern schoolyard is precisely defined by the independent new building
The compact volume maintains the permeability of the complex
Existing outdoor space qualities are largely retained and the path network is supplemented
The entrance is clearly positioned at the open gymnasium courtyard in a loosely planted green area
The listed pavilion in the square creates a good connection between existing break areas and the gym courtyard
The solitaire is a formal reference to the pavilion architecture of the 1950s
The tectonic facade structure and cantilevered roof support this intention
Openings and materialisation are designed to be comprehensible
The concentric internal organisation is efficient and clear
Three cores growing through the building recall a multi-trunked tree
The centrally lit staircase is more than access and also works as seating area, stage or catwalk
The angled shape of each classroom expands the options for furnishing
External connections allowing a circular route across the floor promote close collaboration between classes
Lighting of the basement workrooms is comprehensibly solved via terrain excavations
Two storage rooms in the middle let the day school floor be structured into different areas
The public pavilion allows the school a variety of uses
Views from classroom into corridor in the primary school pavilions are welcomed
A relatively compact structure with a simple insulation perimeter
Interventions in the existing buildings remain minimal except for one pavilion
The design responds to the complex task with urban precision and architectural sensitivity
negative: The staircase platforms could become too crowded at peak times
Too little space is given to the necessary checkrooms in front of the classrooms
The group rooms as extensions of the classrooms offer only limited cross-class clustering
The rooms adjacent to the day school are hardly suitable while the more suitable rooms sit in another building
Secondary school pupils have to walk longer distances during breaks
Adaptations are required to use a multi-purpose room temporarily as a classroom
In the existing pavilions the group rooms are not optimally positioned between the classrooms
The solution for room acoustics remains unclear and could restrict room dimensions
The building technology concept is compliant but rather complex
The feasibility of the new heat generation in the listed pavilion cannot be verified
Temporary solutions and additional costs are expected during construction
Higher construction costs result from the degree of intervention in the existing buildings
The typological and functional approach to contemporary schooling is not entirely convincing
